4_native_fit_no_sysmem_spill.status: PASS expected -- comfortable headroom, second-best fit of the six
4_native_fit_no_sysmem_spill.evidence: epoch-1 gemma-v2 measured 12.5 GiB allocated / 22.2 GiB reserved against a 23.889 GiB ceiling -- 1.7 GiB of headroom. A real measurement at the identical configuration.
4_native_fit_no_sysmem_spill.why_not_probe_based: the 12-step probe reports 12.4/15.5 GiB. All three prior probes underpredicted (granite 16.9 vs 24.6; phi 10.8 vs 28.4; qwen 13.1 vs 18.1), so the probe confirms only the trainable count and step time.
4_native_fit_no_sysmem_spill.caveat: across three completed epoch-2 runs, reserved memory drifted materially only where the allocator was already saturated (phi +2.1 GiB at 26.3 -> 28.4; granite 0.0 at 24.6; qwen +0.1 at 18.0 -> 18.1). Gemma sits 1.7 GiB UNDER the ceiling, which is less margin than qwen had, so a phi-like drift could push it over. Not predicted either way -- the full training log is the authoritative record. This is the gate most likely to be surprised.

watch_item_specific_to_gemma: Gemma epoch-1 sits at 8/7/6 on the robustness holdout -- the only one of the four run so far that was NOT already near a terminal state. Granite (2/3/4), Phi (11/2/1) and Qwen (12/5/0) all converged to 12/0/0 or 12/0/1 after a second epoch. Gemma is therefore the first genuine chance to see whether boundary collapse is universal or has an exception. Its failure mode is also distinct: reasoning-leakage / CoT-contaminated JSON on difficult cases, not the magnitude-triggered comma formatting granite and phi showed.
